summary:
Near the Moon's south pole the Sun never climbs more than a few degrees, so a hill kilometres away decides whether a lander has power, and Earth's position decides whether it can talk home. In March 2025, IM-2 Athena landed in a cold crater and its panels never recharged.

Moonset is a web app that answers one question for any landing site and date: will the Sun and Earth be above the real horizon when you land? It traces each spot's skyline from NASA LRO laser-altimeter terrain, places the Sun and Earth with JPL's DE440 ephemeris, and gives a plain-language verdict with sunset and Earthset countdowns, Sun elevation, sunlight %, Earth-in-view %, longest night and energy per square metre.

Planners pick from 42 curated sites (Apollo, CLPS, Luna, Chang'e, Chandrayaan-3, SLIM, Artemis III regions) or click any point, compare up to four candidates, find the best landing dates, and get ranked alternates within seconds when a launch slips. Educators and the public get a live sky view, a 3D globe and a first-person walk on NASA's 5 m terrain. Every number is computed live in the browser and checked against JPL Horizons and published illumination studies.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Moonset is a lunar landing-site navigator. Pick any of 42 curated sites or click any point on the Moon, choose a date, and it tells you in one plain sentence whether the Sun and Earth will be above the real horizon, then shows the numbers behind that answer:

• Sun elevation (shown first), countdowns to sunset, sunrise, Earthset and Earthrise

• Sunlight %, Earth-in-view %, longest night, longest gap in line of sight to Earth, energy per square metre

• Best landing dates, landing-area slope, and touchdown risk from 360 simulated landings

• A six-step planner: pick candidates, find dates, compare side by side, lock the plan against power and line-of-sight checks, re-plan when "something changed" (launch slip or lost site → ranked alternates within seconds), and export to text, CSV, JSON or calendar

HOW IT WORKS

A Python pipeline turns raw NASA products into compact files. In the browser, the engine ray-traces NASA terrain in 720 directions out to 150 km, including lunar curvature, to build each spot's skyline. It compares that skyline with Sun and Earth directions from JPL's DE440 ephemeris (NAIF SPICE), sampled every 2 hours from 2019 to 2036. Earth counts as "in view" only when its whole disc is at least 2° above the skyline. Rise and set events are found to the minute. One rule holds the app together: all physics lives in one engine, so the map, sky view, planner and assistant always show the same numbers.

VISUALIZATIONS

2D south-pole map with live shadows and sunlight/Earth-view heat layers, whole-Moon map, 3D globe, eye-level sky view with true-size Sun and Earth, and a first-person 3D walk on 5 m terrain at Malapert Massif, Connecting Ridge and Leibnitz Beta. Press play and the shadows move.

FOR EVERY SKILL LEVEL

Simple mode uses plain words, finger-widths and local time. Expert mode shows UTC, degrees, uncertainty ranges and battery/load inputs. Same maths, two vocabularies. Light and dark themes, phone and desktop.

ACCURACY

Sun direction within 0.0002° and Earth within 0.006° of JPL Horizons (23 dates). Connecting Ridge sunlight 93.3% vs 92.3% published (Gläser et al. 2014). Shackleton crater floor 0% (permanently shadowed, Mazarico et al. 2011). Held-out cross-validation against Bussey et al. 2010: 5.5 ± 3.8 percentage points. At seven independent points from Barker et al. 2021 that we never tuned on, the 80 m model reads 0.7–2.1 points above their conservative values; the app shows both terrain models and flags spots where they disagree.

LIMITS WE SHOW IN THE APP

Away from the pole the skyline uses a ~1.9 km global map. "Earth in view" is line of sight, not a full radio link. Energy uses simple panel assumptions. 5 m terrain covers three regions.

IMPACT

Mission planners get answers in seconds instead of juggling Quickmap, Moon Trek and JPL Horizons, plus a plan that survives a launch slip. Educators can show why the pole is different. Anyone can stand on the Moon in a browser.

TOOLS

JavaScript, HTML, CSS and three.js (static web app, no server); Python with NumPy, rasterio, SpiceyPy and Pillow for the data pipeline; Node engine tests and a Playwright browser test suite; GitHub Pages hosting. Open source under the MIT licence.

TEAM

Team Binary: Muhammad Asjed and Zainab Bilal.
